1:
What the opening phrase reaches back to is the first quarrel. Gill rules out the Gospel, since a message is not seen with bodily eyes or handled with hands, and carries the words past the prophets, Abraham and Adam, to everlasting; Wesley says the phrase properly means from eternity, being equivalent with the in the beginning of John 1:1; Clarke reads it of that glorious personage who was from eternity; Robertson notes the phrase is anarthrous as in the Gospel and holds that it reaches beyond the Christian dispensation and beyond the Incarnation to the eternal purpose of God in Christ, coeval in some sense with creation. Calvin dissents outright: it is more consistent with the passage to take the words of the beginning of the Gospel and of our Saviour's ministry, since what was from the beginning is what the apostles heard and saw — and the other reading, he says, was adopted through an over-anxiety, in many and especially in the Fathers, to establish a divinity which the next verse establishes well enough by itself. Barnes reaches the same conclusion by another route, that the phrase here means from the commencement of the manifestation and not, as in the Gospel, from eternity.

Whether the relative is personal is a second question. Robertson holds that strictly the neuter is not personal but stands for the message concerning the Word of life; Barnes makes the same grammatical point sharper, that John would have written the masculine had he meant to apply the term directly to the Son, and that what is in view is whatever about the incarnate Saviour could be submitted to the senses. Augustine takes it personally and asks who handles the Word with hands, unless because the Word was made flesh — the flesh beginning of the Virgin Mary, though the Word did not then begin. His explanation of the manifesting is the finest thing here: it was from the beginning, only not manifested to men, being manifested to the angels who fed on it as their bread; and the Life was manifested in flesh so that what can be seen only by the heart should be seen by the eyes also — for we had wherewith to see the flesh but not wherewith to see the Word. Henry adds that the Gospel disjoins the two titles while the epistle conjoins them: he is the vital Word, not a bare uttered word but a living one.

Henry enumerates four senses: the ear, since the apostles attended the ministry above three years; the eye, which saw him at the transfiguration, dying and risen; the inward eye, since which we have looked upon is applied not to the immediate object of sight but to what was rationally collected from it; and the hand, referring to the proof given after the resurrection, when Thomas was called before the rest to satisfy his unbelief. Those who resolve the whole into hearing the gospel, he says, lose both the variety of the sensations and the propriety of the words. Robertson turns the catalogue against the Docetists, since with our eyes excludes an optical illusion and the verb for handling is the one Jesus used to prove he was no mere spirit. Clarke presses the tenses the same way: they looked on him not transiently but frequently, and frequently touched his person.

Calvin asks why so much is heaped up at once, and answers that since our salvation depends on the gospel its certainty is in the highest degree necessary, and to believe is not lightly to form an opinion but to hold a firm and undoubting conviction. Henry begins further back, with the apostle's omission of his own name, either from humility or from willingness that the reader be swayed by the weight of the things written rather than the name.
2:
Robertson treats the verse as an important parenthesis, a mark of John's style as at John 1:15, by which the writer heaps reassurance on his statement of the reality of the Incarnation: the verb for manifesting makes known what already exists, whether invisible or visible; the witnessing and the announcing are both present indicatives, the second being the public proclamation of great news; the relative is qualitative, meaning which very life; and the clause about the Father uses not the verb of becoming but the verb of being, with a preposition of intimate fellowship, precisely as at the opening of the Gospel. He notes that the parenthesis closes by repeating the word it began with.

Calvin allows the sense to be twofold — that Christ, who is life and the fountain of life, has been manifested, or that life has been openly offered to us in him — the second following from the first, though the two differ as cause and effect; and he takes the repetition to speak of the effect, that life is obtained for us in Christ. He then distinguishes the eternal possession from the exercise: the power of giving life belonged always to the eternal wisdom of God, but was not actually exercised before the creation, and only when God began to exhibit the Word did what had been hidden diffuse itself over all created things. Manifestation there had already been, but life was manifested at length when Christ completed the work of redemption in our flesh; the fathers under the law shared the same life, yet were shut up under a hope not yet revealed, seeking life from a death and resurrection remote from their eyes and hidden from their minds, whereas we hold already revealed the one whom they had only in types. The whole object, he says, is to remove any suspicion of novelty that might lessen the dignity of the Gospel: life had not now begun to be, though it had lately appeared, for it was always with the Father.

Gill fixes the same point in the divine nature, that the Word of life has life as God in and of himself, without derivation and independent of another, and that this living God, invisible from all eternity, was manifested in human nature in the fulness of time. Clarke makes him the creator and the fountain of life to all sentient and intellectual beings, and reads the verse as the apostle's own cross-reference, since he preached this doctrine of eternal life in the Gospel and now confirms it by the epistle. Wesley divides the labour: the apostles testify by declaring, preaching laying the foundation and writing building on it, and the eternal life named here at the beginning is the same that closes the epistle at the end.
3:
Robertson counts this the third occurrence of the formula, resuming after the parenthesis, and calls emphasis by repetition a thoroughly Johannine trait; Calvin gives the reason, that nothing might be wanting as to the real certainty of the doctrine, and observes that the heralds Christ chose were men fit to be witnesses of the very things they had to declare. Calvin also reads the writer's motive out of the sentence: John was moved by nothing but a wish to invite his readers into an inestimable good, so that we must be extremely ungrateful if we refuse to hear a man who offers to share the happiness he has obtained. Clarke makes the same claim negatively — nothing here comes by hearsay, tradition or conjecture.

On the word for fellowship, Barnes defines it as having something in common, partaking or sharing, and then guards the clause about the Father: it cannot mean that the apostle's nature was the same as God's or that in anything he was equal with God, only that he partook in some measure of the same feelings, views, aims and joys, a union of affection, desire and plan. Robertson derives the noun from the word for partner and notes that the preposition stresses mutual relationship, John explaining his own meaning carefully so that the partnership is with the Father and the Son and possible only in Christ. Clarke expands it into a real participation in the grace, peace, love and life of God. Calvin supplies the reason a second clause was needed at all: the ungodly have a mutual union of their own, but it is without God, and serves to alienate them further from him, which is the extreme of all evils — so John shows he wished them associates for no other end than to lead them to God.

The closing clause is disputed in its text. Barnes reports that the best editions now read your joy where the common text had our, and Robertson that the manuscripts differ here as often between the two; Robertson adds that the periphrastic perfect stresses the state of completion, that the joy may remain full. Barnes hears in the phrase almost the words our Lord used before leaving his disciples at John 15:11, and thinks John had them in mind. Calvin makes the fulness a test: where the treasure is the heart will be, and whoever really perceives what fellowship with God is will be satisfied with that alone and burn no more for other things, so that a man has made proficiency in the Gospel when he counts himself happy in communion with God and prefers it to the whole world. Wesley distinguishes a joy of hope, a joy of faith and a joy of love, and takes the joy of faith to be directly meant here; Clarke reads the verse as a promise of something further, since they had already tasted that the Lord is good and were now to be shown the height of their calling; Gill lists what the things written are — the deity and eternity of the Word, the truth of his humanity, and the fellowship of the saints with the Father and the Son.
5:
The word for what is delivered is itself uncertain. Calvin will not disapprove the old rendering annunciation, since the noun most often means a promise but the context here seems to want the wider sense — unless we say that the promise brought has this condition annexed to it — and he notes that the more approved word has been substituted for it, the two being close in meaning. Gill reports that the Syriac simply gives this is the Gospel, while others render it this is the promise, that those who walk in the light shall have communion and others shall not; Robertson observes that the noun occurs only here and once later in the epistle. Barnes fixes the preposition: it does not mean concerning him but from him, so that this is the sum of what was received out of all that he said. Clarke presses the same point further, that neither Moses nor the prophets gave the full instruction about God and communion with him which Christ has given.

Whom the pronoun refers to is settled by position. Henry argues that the Son is both the immediate sender of the apostles and the nearest antecedent in the preceding context, so that the message comes from him; Wesley says the same in three words. Henry adds the dignity of the errand, that apostolic ministers are the messengers of the Lord Jesus and can pretend to nothing higher, and that he who put on human nature will honour earthen vessels.

On the affirmation itself the commentators strain for language. Barnes insists on the absence of the article — not the light, nor a light, but light itself, the source and fountain of light in all worlds, perfectly pure without admixture of sin, all knowledge with no ignorance, infinitely happy with nothing to make him miserable, infinitely true and never countenancing error. Robertson notes that the same is said of the Word in the Gospel and claimed by Jesus for himself. Clarke argues from the properties of the creature, light being the purest, most subtile, most useful and most diffusive of God's works and therefore a fit emblem, and turns it into a comparison: God is to the human soul what light is to the world, and without his indwelling brightness religion is an empty science and a dead letter, the soul a trackless wilderness and a howling waste. Wesley compresses the same into a line, that what light is to the natural eye God is to the spiritual. Henry takes the report to concern the moral perfection we are to imitate, comprehending God's holiness, his penetrative knowledge of hearts, and his justice, which burns as a most bright and vehement flame.

The negative half is read as characteristic and as protective. Barnes calls it much in John's manner, not merely affirming a thing but guarding it so that no mistake can be made, and takes it to assert an absolute perfection which not even the smallest spot could dim, as a spot dims the sun; he suspects it aimed at the error of charging God with the authorship of the sin and misery in the world. Calvin says the same of the style, that John commonly amplifies an affirmation by a contrary negation, and draws the consequence, that God so hates an evil conscience and all that belongs to darkness that as long as we walk in darkness there is a separation between us and him — for the object here was not to give the whole doctrine of the Gospel but to show that whoever would enjoy Christ must be conformed to God in righteousness and holiness. Clarke completes the antithesis from the other side, darkness implying all imperfection, and chiefly ignorance, sinfulness and misery.
6:
The verse turns on a claim that can be made without being true. Gill reads "if we say" as the profession of any claiming to partake of the divine nature and have the light of God's countenance. Wesley presses further: the saying may be "either with our tongue, or in our heart," and the darkness "either inwardly or outwardly." Barnes insists the contradiction is objective, not psychological: such professors are false, but "this does not mean necessarily that they meant to deceive." He also blocks a softer reading of his own day — walking in darkness "now commonly denotes to be in doubt about our religious state," but the leading thought is that a life in sin disproves the profession. Clarke supplies a target, the Gnostics against whose errors he takes the epistle to be written: "great pretenders to knowledge, to the highest degrees of the Divine illumination," whose "manners were excessively corrupt."

Robertson notes a third-class condition with ἐάν and ingressive aorist εἴπωμεν, "up and say." Darkness here is σκότος, not the σκοτία of John 1:5; ψευδόμεθα is present middle, "plain Greek and plain English," like the word about the devil in John 8:44, and "do not the truth" is its negative restatement. Calvin classifies the argument formally as "an argument from what is inconsistent," but refuses to leave it there. The inference rests on a higher principle, "that God sanctifies all who are his." John is not issuing a naked precept requiring holy life; he shows that "the grace of Christ serves for this end to dissipate darkness." What God communicates is no vain fiction: its power must show in the life, or possession of the gospel is fallacious.

Verse 7 states the positive. Barnes unpacks walking in light as three things: a holy life, embracing truth against heathenism and infidelity, and enjoying religion's comforts. "As he is in the light" he qualifies carefully — the measure is not the same in degree, but the light is of the same kind. Calvin faces the difficulty head on: who so exhibits God's light as to be wholly pure? Such expressions are "accommodated to the capacities of men"; he is like God "who aspires to his likeness, however distant from it he may as yet be," and walks in the light "though he may in many things offend and sigh under the burden of the flesh." Integrity of conscience alone distinguishes light from darkness.

The fellowship is disputed textually. Clarke reports versions and manuscripts reading μετ' αὐτοῦ, "with him," rather than μετ' ἀλλήλων, "with each other," and prefers it: "God and a holy heart are in continual correspondence." Barnes keeps the horizontal sense: sharing God's views and ends, believers resemble each other. Robertson keeps it too but reverses the order of dependence: "we cannot have fellowship with one another unless we have it with God in Christ."

On the cleansing blood the division is sharper. Clarke reads καθαρίζει as continuous — it "continues to cleanse us, i.e., to keep clean what it has made clean" — notes manuscripts with the future καθαριεῖ, and holds that cleansing from all sin is what every believer "must have in this life": Christ "is not a partial Savior." Barnes allows only that the blood removes any sin of which we may be conscious, and that its efficacy is available "on the conditions" of repentance and faith. Calvin turns it against Rome: pardon is not given once at baptism with satisfactions after, but is "a benefit perpetually residing in the Church, and daily offered to the faithful"; assigning merit to works "in the least degree" subverts it. John "assigns not the half, but the whole, to the blood of Christ." Robertson guards the word from another side: real blood, "no mere phantom," not the mere example of Jesus. Wesley sums the scope — original and actual, "all the guilt and all the power."
8:
Gill takes the denial as a live danger for believers: cleansed by Christ's blood, they are still not without sin. His evidence: the confessions of saints in every age, their groans, "the continual war in them between flesh and spirit," their prayers for fresh application of Christ's blood, their backslidings. Freed from guilt and from obligation to punishment, they are not freed from sin itself. Henry states the principle flatly: "The Christian religion is the religion of sinners, of such as have sinned, and in whom sin in some measure still dwells"; the Christian life is "a life of continued repentance." Denial, he adds, both deceives us and, at verse 10, dishonours God by challenging his veracity — God having testified to the world's sin by providing a sacrifice needed in all ages.

Clarke and Robertson both read the denial historically. Clarke thinks the heretics addressed "denied that they had any sin, or needed any Savior," and reports the Gnostic doctrine that the Aeon dwelling in Jesus left him at his arrest, so a common man's death "had neither merit nor efficacy." Robertson defines the claim as "no personal guilt, no principle of sin" and traces it to the Gnostic axiom that matter is evil and the soul uncontaminated by flesh. πλανῶμεν is active: we lead ourselves astray, since "we do not deceive others who know us." Barnes suspects an allusion to the Nicolaitanes but will not insist. Calvin reaches instead for the doctrine's history, recalling that Augustine refuted the Pelagians from this verse and "wisely thought that the confession of guilt is not required for humility's sake, but lest we by lying should deceive ourselves."

Barnes turns the verse against a target Clarke defends. The declaration applies, he says, "not only to those who maintain that they have not been guilty of sin in the past, but also to those who profess to have become perfectly sanctified"; such a man "must know little of his own heart." Who, he asks, would go out at midnight under the open heaven and say he was as pure as the God who made those stars? Clarke, on the next verse, says the opposite. Cleansing from all unrighteousness is cleansing from all sin, since all unrighteousness is sin; to plead for sin's continuance through life is "ungrateful, wicked, and even blasphemous"; it is "the birthright of every child of God to be cleansed from all sin." Calvin occupies neither position: the cleansing is real but unfinished. God is faithful to cleanse "not today or tomorrow," for "as long as we are surrounded with flesh, we ought to be in a continual state of progress"; what he has begun he goes on daily to do until he completes it.

The word just divides them again. Barnes objects that it cannot bear its strict sense, since forgiveness "is never an act of justice, but is an act of mercy"; he offers three looser readings, preferring that God is just to his Son in the covenant of redemption. Calvin makes the stronger claim: God "might have been just, were he to deal with us with all the rigor of justice; but as he has bound himself to us by his word, he would not have himself deemed just, except he forgives." Wesley puts it as a feint: "Just — Surely then he will punish: no; for this very reason he will pardon," since when the debt is paid "it is the part of equity to cancel the bond." Clarke divides the remedy: sin exists as guilt requiring pardon and as pollution requiring cleansing, each separately confessed. Gill restricts the confession's direction: faults against neighbours may be owned to them, but sin as such is confessed to God alone, "against whom it is committed, and who only can pardon." Robertson, reading "if we keep on confessing," cites James 5:16 for confession to one another as well.
10:
The tense is the point. Robertson marks οὐχ ἡμαρτήκαμεν as perfect active: verse 8 denied the principle of sin, this verse denies "any specific acts of sin." Barnes reads the pair the same way and draws the inference that closes the loop — since verse 8 speaks of the present and verse 10 of the past, "neither in reference to the past nor the present can any one lay claim to perfection." Gill fills in what the denial has to include to be maintained: it must deny original sin and the doctrine that men are born in sin, must hold that they "come into the world pure and holy," and must assert that concupiscence is not sin, counting only outward acts as sinful and disregarding internal lusts and desires.

The charge is no longer self-deception but slander of God. Barnes grounds it in the sheer weight of testimony: on no point have God's declarations been "more positive and uniform than on the fact of the universal sinfulness of man," and he strings the passages from Genesis and Job through the Psalms to Romans 3. Calvin makes the aggression explicit — one who tries to escape the charge "carries on war with God, and accuses him of falsehood, as though he condemned the undeserving." Robertson relays David Smith's diagnosis of two causes behind the claim to personal perfection: the stifling of conscience, which makes God a liar (ψεύστην, the word Jesus uses of the devil in John 8:44), and ignorance of God's word, which if present would prevent the claim being made at all. Barnes takes "his word is not in us" as equivalent to having no religion, since the whole system rests on man being fallen and needing a Saviour; Calvin turns it toward progress, since we advance in the knowledge of God's word only as we "become really humbled, so as to groan under the burden of our sins."

Barnes closes the chapter with a series of reflections rather than a comment. Two bear on the verse. On confession he is blunt about where the shame lies: "All meanness was in doing the wrong, not in confessing it," so concealment is neither noble nor safe, since no one escapes on the presumption that his sins are unknown. On the terms of pardon he is warmer — no painful sacrifice is demanded, "no penance, pilgrimage, or voluntary scourging," only acknowledgment at the foot of the cross. And he returns to the chapter's opening image to keep "God is light" from being contradicted by experience: a cloud may come between us and the sun, but beyond it the sun shines undimmed, and at midnight the darkness is not the sun "shorn of his beams." Sorrow, on that reading, is cloud rather than evidence.
